title: Data Wrangling Tool
text:
Welcome
Cleaning messy psychology survey data with R & the tidyverse — work your way from raw export to analysable dataset.

title: Data Wrangling Tool
text:
How to use this
Data cleaning usually follows a fairly consistent set of steps — from setting up your project, through importing and checking your data, to saving a clean version ready for analysis. You can work through those steps in order from start to finish, or jump straight to whichever task matches what you’re stuck on right now — whatever’s useful for your data today. Each section ends with real R code you can copy into your script, plus a tip about why it matters.
Before you start, install the packages once: install.packages(c("tidyverse", "janitor", "naniar", "here", "DataExplorer")). Then at the top of every cleaning script: library(tidyverse) loads dplyr, tidyr, readr, and lubridate together; add library(janitor), library(naniar), library(here) and library(DataExplorer) separately.
Start every project as an RStudio Project with separate folders for raw and clean data, and use here() to build file paths (e.g. here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.csv")) instead of typing them out by hand — see Set up your project.

title: Set up your project
text:
Packages: here

Before you write a single line of cleaning code, set up a proper R Project with separate folders for raw and clean data. This keeps your original raw file safe from being overwritten, and — combined with the here package — means your file paths work on any computer, not just yours.
# In RStudio: File > New Project > New Directory > New Project
# This creates a .Rproj file at your project's root folder

# Project folder structure:
#
# my_project/
# |-- my_project.Rproj
# |-- data/
# |   |-- raw/      <- original files, never edited by hand
# |   `-- clean/    <- outputs from your cleaning script
# `-- scripts/
#     `-- 01_clean_data.R

# Inside that project, create the data folders (once):
dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE)
dir.create("data/clean", recursive = TRUE)

# Install the here package once
install.packages("here")
library(here)

# here() builds a path from your project's root, no matter which
# sub-folder your script lives in or who runs it
here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.csv")






Tip



Never hard-code a full file path like "C:/Users/Jen/Desktop/survey.csv" — it will break on anyone else’s computer (including future-you on a new laptop). here() builds paths relative to your project’s root folder instead, so the same script runs anywhere.



Where to next:

Now import my raw data file

title: Import your data
text:
Import a CSV file
read_csv() guesses each column’s type from the data and is far more predictable than base R’s read.csv(). Wrapping the file path in here() means this works whether you run it from a script, a notebook, or someone else’s computer.

title: Import your data
text:
Packages: readr here


library(readr)
library(here)

survey_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.csv"))

# check for anything readr couldn't parse cleanly
problems(survey_raw)






Tip



Always read into a new object (survey_raw) and never edit the CSV by hand. Treat the raw file as untouchable — that’s why it lives in data/raw/.



Where to next:

Now get an overview of it

title: Import your data
text:
Import an Excel file

Packages: readxl here

readxl is part of the wider tidyverse family and pairs naturally with read_csv() — same idea, for .xlsx files.
library(readxl)
library(here)

survey_raw <- read_excel(here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.xlsx"), sheet = 1)






Tip



If your spreadsheet has extra title rows above the real header, add skip = n to skip them.



Where to next:

Now get an overview of it

title: Import your data
text:
Import an SPSS (.sav) file

Packages: haven here

haven is the tidyverse-adjacent package for reading SPSS/Stata/SAS files. SPSS files often store labelled values (e.g. 1 = ‘Male’) as a special haven_labelled type, which you’ll usually want to convert.
library(haven)
library(here)

survey_raw <- read_sav(here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.sav"))

# turn value labels into a proper R factor
survey_raw <- survey_raw |> as_factor()






Tip



Run str(survey_raw) after importing — SPSS files frequently hide useful info in variable/value labels that’s easy to miss.



Where to next:

Now get an overview of it

title: Import your data
text:
Import a Qualtrics export

Packages: readr here

Qualtrics CSV exports have three header rows: variable names, full question text, and an internal ImportId row. You usually want only the first row as your column names.
library(readr)
library(here)

# grab the real variable names from row 1
var_names <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.csv"), n_max = 0) |> names()

# skip the first 3 rows (names, question text, import IDs), reuse var_names
survey_raw <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "survey_raw.csv"), skip = 3, col_names = var_names)






Tip



The qualtRics package is another way around these formatting quirks: use fetch_survey() if you have API access, or read_survey() to read an exported CSV directly — it handles the header rows for you and keeps the question wording as metadata instead of discarding it.

Now get an overview of it

title: Get an overview & spot problems
text:
dplyr
Always do this before any cleaning — it tells you exactly what needs fixing, rather than guessing.
glimpse() gives you a compact, column-by-column view of your data: the variable name, its type, and a peek at the first few values. Scan the type column first — that’s where dates or numbers hiding as text show up — then scan the values themselves for anything that looks off.
crumbs: 3  Get an overview & spot problems

title: Get an overview & spot problems
text:
library(dplyr)

glimpse(survey_raw)
crumbs: 3  Get an overview & spot problems

title: Get an overview & spot problems
text:
naniar
miss_var_summary() ranks every column by how much of it is missing. vis_miss() turns that into a visual grid, so you can see at a glance whether missingness is scattered randomly or concentrated in particular variables or participants — a pattern worth investigating (e.g. everyone who abandoned the survey partway through).
library(naniar)

miss_var_summary(survey_raw)

vis_miss(survey_raw)
crumbs: 3  Get an overview & spot problems

title: Get an overview & spot problems
text:
janitor
tabyl() gives you a frequency table for one categorical column — counts and percentages for every value it contains. Use it to catch typo’d or inconsistently capitalized categories, unexpectedly rare or common groups, and missing-data codes turning up as their own “category.”
library(janitor)

survey_raw |> 
  tabyl(gender)
crumbs: 3  Get an overview & spot problems

title: Clean & rename columns
text:
Clean up messy column names
clean_names() converts column names like “Participant ID” or “Q1_Have you…” into consistent snake_case (participant_id, q1_have_you) so they’re easy and safe to reference in code.

title: Clean & rename columns
text:
Packages: janitor


library(janitor)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |> clean_names()

names(survey_raw)






Tip



Do this immediately after import, before any other cleaning step — every later step depends on knowing the real column names.



Where to next:

Now rename individual variables
Now get an overview
Now deal with missing data

title: Clean & rename columns
text:
Rename individual variables

Packages: dplyr

clean_names() standardizes formatting, but you’ll usually still want clearer names for specific columns — dplyr::rename() takes new_name = old_name pairs. This matters most for survey-platform exports, where columns often arrive named q3, q7, or SQ001.
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  rename(
    participant_age = q3,
    condition_group  = q7
  )

# rename many columns at once using a data dictionary (a lookup table)
name_dictionary <- tibble::tibble(
  old_name = c("q3", "q7"),
  new_name = c("participant_age", "condition_group")
)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  rename_with(
    ~ name_dictionary$new_name[match(., name_dictionary$old_name)],
    .cols = name_dictionary$old_name
  )






Tip



Renaming right after clean_names() means every later step in your script can use clear variable names instead of cryptic survey-platform codes like q3 or SQ001.



Where to next:

Now get an overview

title: Variable types
text:
Check your variable types
A column that should be numeric but shows up as <chr> is one of the most common silent errors in survey data — it usually means at least one row has a stray character in it.

title: Variable types
text:
Packages: dplyr


library(dplyr)
glimpse(survey_raw)   # quick look at every column's type

# or check a single column's class
class(survey_raw$age)






Tip



Do this right after import, and again after cleaning — catching a type problem early saves you from confusing downstream errors like a numeric summary refusing to run.



Where to next:

Fix a character column that should be numeric
Fix an Excel date stored as a number

title: Variable types
section: Convert a character column to numeric
text:
Convert a character column to numeric

Packages: dplyr

as.numeric() silently turns anything it can’t parse into NA. Before you trust the conversion, check which original values failed — that’s usually where the real problem (stray text, a comma, a typo) is hiding.
library(dplyr)

# check which values will fail to convert BEFORE you overwrite the column
survey_raw |>
  filter(is.na(as.numeric(age)) & !is.na(age)) |>
  distinct(age)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))

# check for new NAs introduced by the conversion
sum(is.na(survey_raw$age))






Tip



Run the “which values failed” check before you overwrite the column, not after — once age has been reassigned, the original text values are gone and you can’t see what caused the problem.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Variable types
section: Fix an Excel date stored as a number
text:
Fix an Excel date stored as a number

Packages: janitor

This shows up when a spreadsheet program stores a date as a serial number (e.g. 45678) instead of text — common after copy-pasting from Excel into a CSV.
library(janitor)
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(start_date = excel_numeric_to_date(as.numeric(start_date)))






Tip



If some dates parse and others don’t, check whether the column is a mix of real dates and Excel serial numbers — a common result of copy-pasting data from two different spreadsheets.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Variable types
section: Convert a column to a factor
text:
Convert a column to a factor

Packages: dplyr

Convert grouping/categorical variables (like experimental condition) to factors before modeling — many R modeling functions treat factors differently from plain character columns.
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(condition = as.factor(condition))

# check the levels
levels(survey_raw$condition)






Tip



If the order of levels matters (e.g. “Low” < “Medium” < “High”), set it explicitly with factor(condition, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")) rather than relying on alphabetical order.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Missing data
text:
Check how missingness is coded
Psychology surveys often use out-of-range numbers (999, -99, -1) to mean ‘missing’ rather than a true blank cell. Spotting these before analysis is essential — otherwise R will treat them as real scores.

title: Missing data
text:
Packages: naniar dplyr


library(naniar)
miss_var_summary(survey_raw)   # official NAs per column
vis_miss(survey_raw)

# eyeball one column's actual values for suspicious codes
library(dplyr)
survey_raw |> count(mood_rating)






Tip



Check your study’s codebook — researchers usually document which numeric code means ‘missing’ for each measure.



Where to next:

They’re already blank/NA
They’re coded as numbers

title: Missing data
section: Convert coded missing values to real NA
text:
Convert coded missing values to real NA

Packages: naniar

naniar’s replace_with_na() turns specific values into proper NA, so dplyr/tidyr functions recognise them as missing instead of as real data.
library(naniar)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  replace_with_na(replace = list(
    age = c(-99, 999),
    mood_rating = c(-99)
  ))

# or apply the same missing code to every column at once
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  replace_with_na_all(condition = ~ .x %in% c(-99, 999))






Tip



Keep a note of which codes you replaced — it belongs in your methods write-up, not just your script.



Where to next:

Now decide what to do about the missing values

title: Missing data
section: Decide what to do about missing values
text:
Decide what to do about missing values

Packages: tidyr dplyr naniar

Once missing values are properly coded as NA, you have a few options depending on your design.
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

# remove rows with ANY missing value
survey_complete <- survey_raw |> drop_na()

# remove rows missing on specific key variables only
survey_complete <- survey_raw |> drop_na(age, condition)

# flag participants with a lot of missing data instead of dropping automatically
library(naniar)
survey_raw |>
  mutate(pct_missing = rowMeans(is.na(across(everything()))) * 100) |>
  filter(pct_missing > 50)






Tip



Don’t drop_na() the whole dataset by default — think about whether missingness is random or meaningful (e.g. someone quit the survey early) before deciding how to handle it.



Where to next:

Now get a final overview

title: Dates & durations
text:
Parse a date column
lubridate’s parsing functions are named after the order your dates appear in: y = year, m = month, d = day. Pick the one matching your raw format.

title: Dates & durations
text:
Packages: lubridate


library(lubridate)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(start_date = ymd(start_date))     # format: 2026-07-01
  # mutate(start_date = mdy(start_date))   # format: 07/01/2026
  # mutate(start_date = dmy(start_date))   # format: 01/07/2026
  # mutate(start_time = ymd_hms(start_time)) # includes a time stamp

# check nothing failed to parse
sum(is.na(survey_raw$start_date))






Tip



A sudden jump in NAs after parsing usually means you picked the wrong order (e.g. used mdy() on day-first dates).



Where to next:

Now extract year/month/weekday
Now calculate age

title: Dates & durations
section: Calculate age from date of birth
text:
Calculate age from date of birth

Packages: lubridate dplyr

Subtracting dates gives you days, so convert to years using lubridate’s time_length() for an accurate result (it accounts for leap years).
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(
    dob = ymd(dob),
    age_years = time_length(interval(dob, today()), "years")
  )






Tip



Round with floor(age_years) if you want age in completed years rather than a decimal.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Dates & durations
text:
Calculate survey duration

Packages: lubridate

Useful for spotting participants who rushed through (likely low-quality data) or who left the survey open for hours.
library(lubridate)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(
    start_time = ymd_hms(start_time),
    end_time   = ymd_hms(end_time),
    duration_mins = time_length(interval(start_time, end_time), "minutes")
  )






Tip



Filter out implausible durations as a data-quality check, e.g. filter(duration_mins < 1) for a survey that should take 20+ minutes.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Dates & durations
text:
Extract parts of a date

Packages: lubridate dplyr

Handy for grouping participants by data collection wave, or checking for day-of-week effects.
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(
    year    = year(start_date),
    month   = month(start_date, label = TRUE),
    weekday = wday(start_date, label = TRUE)
  )






Tip



label = TRUE gives you readable labels (“Jan”, “Mon”) instead of plain numbers.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Recoding & scale scores
text:
Convert coded values to labels
case_when() is the modern, recommended way to do this in dplyr (it’s clearer with multiple conditions and is now preferred over the older recode() function).

title: Recoding & scale scores
text:
Packages: dplyr


library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(gender = case_when(
    gender == 1 ~ "Male",
    gender == 2 ~ "Female",
    gender == 3 ~ "Nonbinary/other",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))






Tip



Always include a fallback line (TRUE ~ NA_character_) so unexpected values become a visible NA instead of silently disappearing.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Recoding & scale scores
text:
Reverse-score a Likert item

Packages: dplyr

The general formula for reverse-scoring is: reversed = (scale minimum + scale maximum) − original score.
library(dplyr)

# example: a 1–5 Likert item, so min + max = 6
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(item3_r = 6 - item3)






Tip



Double-check your scale’s actual min and max before using this formula — a 0–4 scale uses 4, not 6.



Where to next:

Now build a scale score

title: Recoding & scale scores
section: Build a scale score from items
text:
Build a scale score from items

Packages: dplyr

across() lets you average (or sum) several item columns at once into a single total score.
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(anxiety_total = rowMeans(across(c(item1, item2, item3_r, item4)), na.rm = TRUE))

# or a sum instead of a mean:
# mutate(anxiety_total = rowSums(across(c(item1, item2, item3_r, item4)), na.rm = TRUE))






Tip



Reverse-score any relevant items first (previous step) before averaging them into a total — otherwise the scale score will be wrong.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Recoding & scale scores
text:
Recode based on a condition

Packages: dplyr

case_when() evaluates conditions top-to-bottom and uses the first one that matches — great for turning a continuous variable into groups.
library(dplyr)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age < 18 ~ "under 18",
    age >= 18 & age < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age >= 30 & age < 50 ~ "30-49",
    age >= 50 ~ "50+",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))






Tip



Order matters — case_when() stops at the first TRUE condition, so put more specific rules earlier.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Reshape wide & long
text:
Reshape wide to long
Long format — one row per observation — is what most repeated-measures ANOVAs and mixed-effects models in R expect.

title: Reshape wide & long
text:
Packages: tidyr


library(tidyr)

survey_long <- survey_raw |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("trial"),
    names_to = "trial",
    values_to = "rt"
  )






Tip



cols accepts helpers like starts_with(), contains(), or just a plain vector of column names.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Reshape wide & long
text:
Reshape long to wide

Packages: tidyr

Useful when you need one row per participant for a correlation matrix or a simple summary table.
library(tidyr)

survey_wide <- survey_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = trial,
    values_from = rt
  )






Tip



pivot_wider() and pivot_longer() are exact inverses — if something looks wrong, try reversing the operation to see where it breaks.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Inclusion & exclusion
text:
Filter rows to keep — inclusion criteria
Use filter() when you can describe who you want to KEEP. Watch out: filter() treats NA like FALSE, so rows with a missing value on your filtering variable get silently dropped too — not just the rows that truly fail the criteria.

title: Inclusion & exclusion
text:
Packages: dplyr


library(dplyr)

# keep only participants who consented and are 18+
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  filter(consent == "Yes", age >= 18)






Tip



Because filter() drops NA rows on the condition, always compare nrow() before and after, and check whether anyone was dropped only because of a missing value rather than truly failing the criteria.



Where to next:

See the drop-focused version (filter_out)
Now check your data is clean

title: Inclusion & exclusion
text:
Filter rows out — exclusion criteria

Packages: dplyr

filter_out(), added in dplyr 1.2.0, is the companion to filter() built specifically for describing who you want to REMOVE. Unlike a negated filter() (using !condition), filter_out() treats NA like FALSE too — so participants with a missing value on your exclusion variable are correctly kept rather than accidentally dropped. Requires dplyr 1.2.0 or later (packageVersion("dplyr") to check).
library(dplyr)

# drop anyone who withdrew consent, or failed the attention check
survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  filter_out(consent == "Withdrew", attention_check == "Failed")

# compare: the old, error-prone way to write the same thing with filter()
# survey_raw |> filter(!(consent == "Withdrew" & attention_check == "Failed"))
# ...that version silently mishandles any row with an NA in either column






Tip



Reach for filter_out() any time you catch yourself writing != or wrapping a condition in !( ) to describe who to exclude — that’s exactly the pattern it replaces.



Where to next:

See the keep-focused version (filter)
Now check your data is clean

title: Inclusion & exclusion
text:
Apply a full inclusion/exclusion checklist

Packages: dplyr

Most studies apply both at once — keep the eligible, then drop the excluded. Doing this as two explicit steps (rather than one long condition) keeps your criteria easy to read back later, e.g. when writing a participant-flow paragraph for a methods section.
library(dplyr)

n_start <- nrow(survey_raw)

survey_raw <- survey_raw |>
  # inclusion: keep only eligible participants
  filter(consent == "Yes", age >= 18) |>
  # exclusion: drop anyone who should be removed even if eligible
  filter_out(attention_check == "Failed", duplicate_flag == TRUE)

n_end <- nrow(survey_raw)
n_start - n_end   # how many participants were removed






Tip



Keep a running count like n_start/n_end for every inclusion/exclusion step — it’s exactly the number you’ll need for a CONSORT-style participant flow description.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Duplicates
text:
Packages: janitor dplyr

Duplicate participant IDs can mean a participant submitted twice, a data entry error, or sometimes a genuine repeated-measures row — check before deleting.
library(janitor)

# see the actual duplicate rows
survey_raw |> get_dupes(participant_id)

library(dplyr)
# keep only the first occurrence of each ID
survey_raw <- survey_raw |> distinct(participant_id, .keep_all = TRUE)






Tip



Investigate why a duplicate exists before deleting it — it might be a legitimate second session, not an error.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Combine files
text:
Stack files with matching columns
bind_rows() stacks data frames on top of each other, matching by column name (filling any column that’s missing in one file with NA).

title: Combine files
text:
Packages: readr dplyr here


library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(here)

batch1 <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "batch1.csv"))
batch2 <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "batch2.csv"))

all_data <- bind_rows(batch1, batch2)






Tip



Run clean_names() on each file first — bind_rows() matches by exact column name, so inconsistent naming will create extra columns instead of an error.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Combine files
text:
Merge files by participant ID

Packages: dplyr here

left_join() keeps every row from your first (left) dataset and attaches matching columns from the second wherever the ID matches.
library(dplyr)
library(here)

demographics   <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "demographics.csv"))
survey_scores  <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "survey_scores.csv"))

full_data <- left_join(demographics, survey_scores, by = "participant_id")

# check for participants that didn't find a match
full_data |> filter(is.na(survey_score))






Tip



If row counts look wrong after joining, check for duplicate IDs in either file first — they cause joins to multiply rows unexpectedly.



Where to next:

Now check your data is clean

title: Check your data is clean
text:
Packages: dplyr janitor naniar

A short checklist to re-run every time you update your cleaning script, before you trust the data enough to analyse it.
library(dplyr)

# range checks — anything outside a plausible range?
survey_raw |> filter(age < 0 | age > 100)
survey_raw |> filter(if_any(starts_with("item"), ~ . < 1 | . > 5))

# unique participant IDs?
library(janitor)
survey_raw |> get_dupes(participant_id)

# any missingness left unaccounted for?
library(naniar)
vis_miss(survey_raw)






Tip



Save these checks as their own short script — re-running it every time you touch the raw data catches problems early.



Where to next:

Now save the clean data
crumbs: 13  Check your data is clean

title: Save your clean data
text:
Packages: readr here

survey_raw has been modified in place at every step so far — this is the one point where it gets a new name. Calling it survey_clean here marks it as finished: ready for analysis, not to be edited by hand. The goal of reproducible cleaning is that you could delete survey_clean.csv entirely and regenerate it perfectly by re-running your script.
library(readr)
library(here)

survey_clean <- survey_raw

write_csv(survey_clean, here("data", "clean", "survey_clean.csv"))






Tip



Never hand-edit survey_clean.csv. If you spot an error, fix it in the cleaning script and re-run the whole thing from the raw file. Keeping raw and clean files in separate folders (data/raw/ vs data/clean/) makes it obvious at a glance which file is safe to overwrite.



Done. That’s the end of this path — your data should now be ready to analyse.

title: Get an overview & spot problems
text:
DataExplorer
Try plot_histogram() to look for crazy values in continuous variables, plot_bar() to find coding errors in categorical variables, and plot_missing() to look at where your data is missing unexpectedly.
library(DataExplorer)

survey_raw |> 
  plot_histogram()
  
survey_raw |> 
  plot_bar()
  
survey_raw |> 
  plot_missing()
  






Tip



Re-run glimpse(), vis_miss(), tabyl() and/or the plot_x() functions after each cleaning step, not just at the start — it’s the fastest way to confirm a fix actually worked.








NoteWhat kind of problems are you looking for?






Wrong variable types — a date or number showing up as <chr> (text), usually caused by a stray character, symbol, or an Excel serial number.
Column names that aren’t meaningful — survey-platform codes like q3, Q7, or SQ001 instead of descriptive names.
Suspicious numeric values that are probably missing-data codes in disguise — things like -99, 999, or -1 sitting in an otherwise 1-5 range.
Wide data that needs to be long (or vice versa) — repeated trials or timepoints spread across separate columns instead of stacked into rows for plotting/modeling.
Extra columns you don’t need — survey-platform metadata like IP address, browser info, or progress percentage that came along with the export.
Columns that are entirely (or almost entirely) missing — often an unused survey question or something that didn’t export properly.
Inconsistent category labels within the same variable — "Female", "female", and "FEMALE" being treated as three different groups.
An unexpected number of rows — more or fewer than you expected can mean a duplicated import, a botched merge, or test/preview responses left in the file.
Implausible values — ages over 100, ratings outside the scale’s range, reaction times of 9999ms — worth a first skim even before the formal validation step later.
One column doing two jobs — e.g. a single field holding multiple “select all that apply” answers separated by commas.
